title: moltbook.com heartbeat skill: unattended auto-update pulls remote instructions and handles the API key in plaintext
summary: Not a malicious skill, but a widely deployed one whose design gives its operator a standing remote-instruction channel. Snyk's technical report documents the moltbook.com heartbeat skill — a skill that runs unsupervised every few hours — as combining remote prompt execution via an auto-update mechanism with improper credential handling (the agent must handle the moltbook API key in plaintext). The report states that this pattern would allow moltbook.com's operator to hijack its entire user base of 1.5 million users by serving malicious instructions through the update channel.
details:
**The pattern:** the published skill is benign at review time; at run time it fetches instructions from an operator-controlled endpoint and follows them. Review-time analysis (registry vetting, human reading, one-off scanning) is therefore structurally unable to bound the skill's behaviour — the effective payload lives on remote infrastructure and can change at any moment, including after the skill has been approved. Snyk measures this "unverifiable dependencies / remote prompt-or-code execution" pattern in 2.9% of clawhub.ai skills and 21% of confirmed malicious samples.

**Compounding factor:** the heartbeat runs unattended on a schedule, so there is no human in the loop when the fetched instructions are executed, and the plaintext API key is available in the same context.

**Why it is in the advisory database:** SkillGate's lockfile pins file content, but a skill that pulls its instructions at run time defeats content pinning by design — the bytes never change. This entry exists so that users can decide against such skills explicitly rather than assume a green scan means bounded behaviour. See docs/THREAT-MODEL.md, "Residual risks".

**Fact vs. inference:** the description of the heartbeat prompt, the two co-occurring issues and the 1.5 million user figure are as published in Snyk's technical report (2026-02-05, Section 4 and Figure 2). No malicious use of the channel has been reported, and none is alleged here. Verified 2026-08-04.
